Theology and Religious Studies at VU Amsterdam examines religious traditions, beliefs, texts and practices, and their place in society. This comparison uses the 2026–2027 Religion and Worldviews route, which combines study of several traditions with philosophy, social perspectives and research. The selected offering is part-time.

UCR offers a broader combination of philosophy, myth, cultural interpretation and belief in public life. It does not reproduce VU’s sustained study of religious traditions, sacred texts and religion-specific research. Shared rows indicate limited content relationships; blank cells preserve important differences. The UCR programme is not professional training for ministry or spiritual care.

Academic year: 2026–2027

External pathway: Religion and Worldviews; Dutch part-time offering

The 180-EC VU curriculum is paced over six calendar years. Teaching is mainly Dutch in the first two academic stages and English in the selected third stage. The newer route advertised for 2027 is not substituted here.

This is a broader response rather than a specialist theology or comparative-religion curriculum.

modals.text:
World Myth & Literature
Investigates myths from around the world—from Gilgamesh to the Ramayana, Greek and Norse myths. Explores how myths underpin literature and connects them to contemporary global cultures.
Close

Philosophy of Mind
Examines historical and modern work on the philosophy of mind. Discusses Descartes’ dualism, the nature of consciousness, AI and animal minds, personal identity, transformative experiences and the influence of technology on experience.
Close

Heritage & Ancient Democracy
In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century. Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants. This course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of political decision-making.
Close

EUR combines public-administration theory and policy analysis with law, economics, sociology, management, a required public-sector internship and a bachelor project. UCR offers related interdisciplinary study, with a second option focused on sustainability governance. It does not reproduce the dedicated policy, internship and bachelor-project sequence. Shared rows include partial content relationships; blank cells show deliberate gaps. Optional independent research is additional to the displayed 180 EC.

Explore the UCR Program Builder ↗

modals.text:
Governance of Sustainability
This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
Close

Psychology of Organizations & Leadership
This course offers Liberal Arts and Sciences students a deep dive into the psychological, social, and structural dynamics that shape workplaces. Through interactive case discussions, simulations, and real-world insights, students develop critical skills in motivation, leadership, group dynamics, and culture. By synthesizing research and applying theory to practice, participants gain the tools to navigate and influence diverse organizational environments effectively.
Close

Econometrics
Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
Close

In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
